title: Recognising dying and the Priorities for Care
blurb: Recognise when someone may be entering the last days of life, review it daily and plan care around the five Priorities.
question: Mr Brennan, 83, has end-stage kidney disease and has chosen not to have dialysis. Since the weekend he sleeps most of the day, takes almost nothing by mouth and his breathing pauses, then quickens. His daughter asks the nurse, 'Is he dying?' What should guide the nurse's response and next steps?

teach.h: Recognising the last days of life
teach.body: NICE NG31 asks professionals to recognise when a person may be entering the last days of life, or may be deteriorating, stabilising or improving even temporarily. It is often difficult to be certain someone is dying, so this is a clinical judgement made by the team using signs, symptoms, function and what the person and family report. In plain English: notice the change, say it out loud as a team, keep checking whether you were right.

teach.caption: Other functional changes: less communication and deteriorating mobility or performance status.

teach.body: Monitor for further changes at least every 24 hours and update the care plan. Improvement in signs, symptoms or function could mean the person is stabilising or recovering, so the plan must change with them. When there is a high level of uncertainty, for example conflicting signs, seek advice from colleagues more experienced in end of life care. Avoid investigations unlikely to change care in the last days, unless there is a clinical need.

teach.h: Five Priorities for Care of the Dying Person (2014)
teach.caption: Leadership Alliance for the Care of Dying People, One chance to get it right (June 2014). The plan covers food and drink, symptom control, and psychological, social and spiritual support.

teach.h: Communicating that someone may be dying
items: Discuss the prognosis with the dying person as soon as it is recognised, unless they do not wish to be told; include those important to them if the person wishes.
Choose the team member to explain it on competence, confidence and rapport with the person, not seniority alone.
Explore their understanding, fears, wishes and spiritual or cultural needs; give accurate information, including about uncertainty.
Record the discussion and share it with the multiprofessional team.

teach.h: Who does what in the last days (NG31)

rows.label: Wishes unmet?
values: Works to meet them where possible

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Brennan on the renal ward
teach.body: Nurse Aisha notes that Mr Brennan, 83, is harder to rouse, has stopped eating and has Cheyne-Stokes breathing. She raises it at the board round; the team agree he may be entering the last days of life and stop routine daily bloods. The consultant, who has built rapport with him, speaks to Mr Brennan and his daughter, explaining the uncertainty honestly. A named lead nurse is identified, an individualised plan covers mouth care, symptoms and his wish to have his rosary with him, and the plan is reviewed every day.

teach.text: Recognising dying is not a one-way door. If Mr Brennan becomes more alert and starts eating, the team must reassess: he may be stabilising. Don't confuse 'may be dying' with 'is certainly dying', and don't stop reviewing once the plan starts.

items: NG31 signs: agitation, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, falling consciousness, mottled skin, noisy secretions, progressive weight loss.
Symptoms: fatigue, loss of appetite. Function: less communication, worse mobility, social withdrawal.
Reassess at least every 24 hours; improvement may mean stabilising or recovery.
Seek more experienced advice when uncertain; avoid investigations unlikely to change care.
Five Priorities: recognise and communicate, sensitive communication, involve the person, support the family, individual plan of care.
A named lead professional supports shared decision-making; explain when wishes cannot be met.

summary: You can now recognise the signs that a person may be in the last days of life, review that judgement daily and seek help when uncertain. You can also plan care around the five Priorities for Care and communicate prognosis sensitively.

A.q: Which group of findings, taken together, is listed by NICE NG31 as suggesting a person may be entering the last days of life?
options: Raised blood pressure, bounding pulse and warm, flushed skin
Increased appetite, restlessness at night and steady weight gain
Fever, productive cough and a raised white cell count
Mottled skin, Cheyne-Stokes breathing and falling consciousness
A.why: NICE NG31 rec 1.1.2 lists agitation, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, deteriorating consciousness, mottled skin, noisy respiratory secretions and progressive weight loss.

whyNot.0: A raised blood pressure with a bounding pulse suggests circulatory overload or another acute problem, not the dying process.
whyNot.1: Loss of appetite and progressive weight loss are the NG31 changes, the opposite of these.
whyNot.2: These suggest an infection, which may be treatable; they are not NG31 signs of dying.

A.q: Once a team recognises that a person may be in the last days of life, how often, at least, does NICE NG31 recommend monitoring for further changes?
options: Every 4 hours
Every 12 hours
Every 24 hours
Every 72 hours
A.why: NICE NG31 rec 1.1.6: monitor for further changes at least every 24 hours and update the care plan.

whyNot.0: Four-hourly is a monitoring interval for some symptom medicines, not the NG31 minimum for reviewing whether someone is dying.
whyNot.1: Twelve-hourly is the minimum for monitoring clinically assisted hydration, not for this review.
whyNot.3: Every three days is too infrequent; the person's condition can change within a day.

A.q: Which is the first of the five Priorities for Care of the Dying Person?
options: Agree a do not attempt CPR decision with the family
Start a syringe pump for symptom control
Arrange the person's preferred place of death
Recognise dying and communicate this clearly
A.why: Priority 1 is that the possibility the person may die within the next few days or hours is recognised and communicated clearly (Leadership Alliance, 2014).

whyNot.0: CPR decisions matter, but they are not one of the five Priorities.
whyNot.1: A syringe pump is one symptom control option, not a Priority.
whyNot.2: Preferred place of death is explored within the individual plan, not as the first Priority.

B.q: Olive, 87, has advanced dementia and pneumonia. On Monday the team agreed she was probably dying. On Wednesday she is awake, recognises her son and asks for a cup of tea. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue the end of life plan, as the decision has been made
Reassess with the team, as she may be stabilising
Explain to the family that this often happens before death
Restart all her previous medicines and routine blood tests
B.why: NICE NG31 rec 1.1.3: improvement in signs, symptoms or function could indicate the person is stabilising or recovering. The team should reassess and update the plan.

whyNot.0: Recognising dying is reviewed at least daily; it is not a fixed decision.
whyNot.2: Telling the family she is about to die anyway ignores possible recovery and is not based on assessment.
whyNot.3: Restarting everything is premature; a team reassessment decides what she now needs.

B.q: Bogdan, 72, has advanced liver disease. The team now think he may be in his last days and must decide who will talk to him about this. According to NICE NG31, what should this choice be based on?
options: The most senior doctor available on the ward that day
The person who first recorded that he might be dying
The nurse allocated to Bogdan for that shift
The professional's competence, confidence and rapport
B.why: NICE NG31 rec 1.2.2: identify the most appropriate available team member based on their competence, confidence and rapport with the person.

whyNot.0: Seniority alone does not make someone the right person for this conversation.
whyNot.1: Being first to notice is not one of the NG31 criteria.
whyNot.2: Shift allocation is not a criterion; the allocated nurse may or may not be the right person.

B.q: Rashid, 80, is thought to be in his last days. His chart still includes daily full blood counts. What does NICE NG31 recommend?
options: Continue them so any change is detected early
Reduce them to twice a week
Avoid tests unlikely to affect his care
Ask the family to decide whether to continue
B.why: NICE NG31 rec 1.1.4: avoid investigations that are unlikely to affect care in the last few days of life unless there is a clinical need, for example a blood count to guide platelet transfusion to avoid catastrophic bleeding.

whyNot.0: Routine tests that will not change care add burden without benefit.
whyNot.1: Reducing frequency still continues tests that will not change care.
whyNot.3: Families should be involved, but the decision about investigations is clinical and based on need.

C.q: Callum, 76, has advanced COPD. The registrar thinks he is dying, but the consultant notes his oxygen levels are improving and he is more alert. The nurse is unsure which plan to follow. What should happen next?
options: Follow the registrar, who documented the decision first
Seek advice from someone experienced in end of life care
Ask Callum's family which plan they would prefer
Start the end of life plan in case he deteriorates later
C.why: NICE NG31 rec 1.1.7: seek advice from colleagues with more experience of end of life care when there is high uncertainty, such as conflicting clinical signs.

whyNot.0: The order of documentation does not resolve conflicting clinical signs.
whyNot.2: The family's views matter but they cannot settle a clinical uncertainty about prognosis.
whyNot.3: Starting an end of life plan 'just in case' risks withdrawing care from someone who may recover.

C.q: Florence, 89, may be in her last days on a medical ward. She wants to die at home, but no care package can be arranged in time. What does NICE NG31 recommend the nurse does?
options: Avoid mentioning it so that she is not upset
Tell the family to take her home without support
Explain to Florence and her family why it is not possible
Arrange transfer to the nearest hospice without discussion
C.why: NICE NG31 rec 1.3.8: when it is not possible to meet a dying person's wishes, explain the reason why to the dying person and those important to them.

whyNot.0: Avoiding the subject denies her honest information and the chance to make other choices.
whyNot.1: Sending her home without support is unsafe and does not meet her care needs.
whyNot.3: A transfer without discussion ignores her involvement in decisions, which is a Priority for Care.

C.q: Which statement about the individualised care plan for a dying person reflects the Priorities for Care?
options: It is written once on admission and kept unchanged
It covers food, drink, symptoms and spiritual support
It is decided by the consultant and shared after death
It follows a standard pathway used for all patients
C.why: Priority 5: an individual plan of care including food and drink, symptom control, and psychological, social and spiritual support is agreed, coordinated and delivered with compassion. NG31 1.3.7 says it is updated as wishes change.

whyNot.0: The plan is reviewed at least daily and changed as the person's needs and wishes change.
whyNot.2: The plan is created in discussion with the person, those important to them and the team, and shared while they are alive.
whyNot.3: The point is that care is individualised, not a standard pathway for everyone.

reteach.title: Notice, name, keep checking
reteach.question: Recognising dying is a team habit, not a single moment. What are the three parts of that habit?

blocks.body: Notice: the changes in signs (breathing pattern, skin, consciousness, secretions), symptoms (fatigue, appetite) and function (talking less, moving less, withdrawing). Name it: agree as a team that the person may be dying and tell them and their family honestly, including the uncertainty. Keep checking: at least every 24 hours, because some people stabilise or improve.

steps.label: Communicate
steps.sub: person first, family if they wish

blocks.text: The 24-hour review is for the overall judgement and care plan. Twelve hours is the minimum for monitoring clinically assisted hydration. Keep the two numbers apart.

explain.body: NG31 1.1.2: agitation, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, deteriorating consciousness, mottled skin, noisy respiratory secretions and progressive weight loss; plus fatigue and loss of appetite, and functional changes such as less communication, worse mobility and social withdrawal.

test.q: A nurse notices a pattern of breathing in which breaths get deeper, then shallower, then stop briefly before restarting. What is this called?
options: Kussmaul breathing
Cheyne-Stokes breathing
Biot's breathing
Paradoxical chest breathing
test.why: Cheyne-Stokes breathing is a cyclical waxing and waning pattern with pauses; NG31 lists it among signs that a person may be dying.

whyNot.0: Kussmaul breathing is deep, rapid breathing seen in metabolic acidosis such as DKA.
whyNot.2: Biot's breathing is irregular clusters of breaths with pauses, without the gradual waxing and waning.
whyNot.3: Paradoxical breathing is inward chest movement on inspiration, seen with chest injury or respiratory muscle weakness.

explain.body: Monitor at least every 24 hours and update the plan. Improvement may mean stabilising or recovery. Seek more experienced advice if signs conflict. Avoid investigations unlikely to change care.

test.q: When signs about whether a person is dying are conflicting, what does NICE NG31 advise?
options: Seek advice from more experienced colleagues
Repeat a full set of blood tests to clarify
Wait 72 hours before making any plan
Let the family make the final decision on the plan
test.why: NICE NG31 rec 1.1.7: seek advice from colleagues with more experience of end of life care when uncertainty is high.

whyNot.1: NG31 advises avoiding investigations unlikely to change care.
whyNot.2: Waiting three days leaves the person without a plan and is longer than the daily review.
whyNot.3: Families are involved, but a clinical judgement about prognosis is the team's responsibility.

explain.body: 1 Recognise and communicate. 2 Sensitive communication with the person and those important to them. 3 Involve the person in decisions to the extent they want. 4 Support the needs of families and others. 5 Individual plan of care: food and drink, symptoms, psychological, social and spiritual support.

test.q: A nurse checks whether a dying man's wife has somewhere to rest and knows how to reach the ward overnight. Which Priority for Care is this?
options: Recognise and communicate
Involve the person
Support the family
Sensitive communication
test.why: Priority 4: the needs of families and others identified as important to the dying person are actively explored, respected and met as far as possible.

whyNot.0: Priority 1 is about recognising that the person may be dying and saying so clearly.
whyNot.1: Priority 3 concerns the dying person's own involvement in decisions.
whyNot.3: Priority 2 is about sensitive communication, not meeting the family's practical needs.

explain.body: Discuss prognosis as soon as dying is recognised, unless the person does not want to know. Choose who speaks by competence, confidence and rapport. Identify a named lead healthcare professional for shared decision-making. Explain when wishes cannot be met.

items: Person first, family if the person wishes

test.q: Leroy, 58, has capacity. When the doctor starts to talk about his outlook, he says, 'I don't want to know how long I've got.' What should the team do?
options: Tell him anyway, as honesty is required by the Code
Respect his wish and check later if it has changed
Tell his family instead and ask them to decide what to share
Write the prognosis in a letter for him to read later
test.why: NICE NG31 rec 1.2.3: discuss prognosis with the dying person unless they do not wish to be informed. Respect his wish and keep exploring, as wishes can change (rec 1.3.7).

whyNot.0: Being open does not mean forcing information on someone who has declined it.
whyNot.2: Information about Leroy should be shared with family if he wishes, not as a way round his decision.
whyNot.3: A letter still forces the information on him against his stated wish.
